```{r setup}
# Helper: figure path resolution
# Returns PNG for HTML output, PDF for DOCX output
# Returns absolute path for file.exists() checks, relative path for include_graphics()
fig_path <- function(fig_name, return_absolute = FALSE) {
  # Get base name without extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(fig_name)
  
  # Detect output format
  output_format <- NULL
  
  # Method 1: Check knitr's pandoc output format
  pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
  if (!is.null(pandoc_to)) {
    output_format <- pandoc_to
  }
  
  # Method 2: Check for DOCX rendering context
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    docx_indicators <- c(
      knitr::opts_knit$get("quarto.document.format") == "docx",
      grepl("docx", knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format") %||% "", ignore.case = TRUE)
    )
    if (any(docx_indicators, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      output_format <- "docx"
    }
  }
  
  png_name <- paste0(base_name, ".png")
  pdf_name <- paste0(base_name, ".pdf")
  
  # Find the actual file location (use absolute paths for checking)
  png_abs <- NULL
  pdf_abs <- NULL
  
  # Try multiple candidate paths
  candidates_png <- c(
    file.path(figures_dir, png_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "06_visualization", "output", "figures", png_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", png_name),
    # Also try relative paths from current working directory
    file.path("../../../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name)
  )
  
  candidates_pdf <- c(
    file.path(figures_dir, pdf_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "06_visualization", "output", "figures", pdf_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", pdf_name),
    # Also try relative paths from current working directory
    file.path("../../../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name)
  )
  
  for (path in candidates_png) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      png_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_pdf) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      pdf_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  # If return_absolute is TRUE, return absolute path (for file.exists checks)
  if (return_absolute) {
    if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      result <- pdf_abs %||% png_abs
    } else {
      result <- png_abs %||% pdf_abs
    }
    # Return NULL if no file found (file.exists(NULL) will return FALSE)
    return(result)
  }
  
  # Determine relative path based on current working directory
  # From reports/ to project root: reports -> chapter2 -> 07_manuscript -> root (3 levels up)
  # Then down to 06_visualization/output/figures
  if (basename(getwd()) == "reports" || grepl("/reports$", getwd())) {
    rel_path <- "../../../06_visualization/output/figures"
  } else {
    rel_path <- "06_visualization/output/figures"
  }
  
  # Return relative path for rendering
  if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, pdf_name))
    } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, png_name))
    }
  } else {
    # HTML: use relative path
    if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, png_name))
    } else if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, pdf_name))
    }
  }
  
  # Fallback
  warning("Figure not found: ", fig_name)
  return(file.path(rel_path, if (!is.null(png_abs)) png_name else pdf_name))
}
```

# Introduction

## Physical–Cognitive Demands and Aging

People routinely make fine perceptual judgments while sustaining physical effort. A surgeon holds steady muscle tension while discriminating tissue boundaries, an athlete tracks a moving target while controlling posture, and an older adult crosses a busy street while carrying groceries. When two demanding tasks compete for limited cognitive resources, performance in one or both can degrade [@wickens2008; @pashler1994dual]. Aging compounds the cost. Older adults contend with both reduced cognitive capacity and a steeper physiological price for effortful engagement [@salthouse1996; @verhaeghen2003].

A shared neuromodulatory system plausibly links the physical and cognitive sides of this interaction. The locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC–NE) system regulates arousal and tunes neural gain, sensory signal-to-noise, and response caution according to task demand and internal state [@astonjones2005; @mather2016; @jepma2012neural]. Characterizing how effort reshapes cognition through this system takes more than overall accuracy or mean reaction time. It means asking which part of the perceptual decision changes: the quality of the sensory evidence itself, or the tendency to favor one response over another.

The present study addresses that question in older adults. It combines a physical–cognitive dual-task with pupillometry and psychometric-function analysis. Effort condition supplies the experimental manipulation of arousal, trial-by-trial pupil state indexes momentary arousal, and the psychometric function distinguishes a change in perceptual sensitivity from a change in response tendency. Together these tools let us ask not only whether effort affects discrimination, but how.

## Quantifying Perceptual Sensitivity

Perceptual sensitivity is best captured by the full intensity–response relationship, not a single accuracy score. A psychometric function (PF) describes how the probability of a given judgment changes as stimulus intensity varies. In the same–different discrimination tasks used here, the PF maps a continuous intensity dimension, frequency offset for audition or contrast difference for vision, onto the probability of responding "different" [@wichmann2001psychometric; @green1966signal; @prins2016psychophysics]. In its probit form it can be written as

$$P(\text{"different"} | X) = \Phi\left(\frac{X - \alpha}{\beta}\right)$$ {#eq-psychometric}

where $X$ is stimulus intensity, $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution, $\alpha$ is a location parameter, and $\beta$ is a scale parameter that sets the slope. A smaller $\beta$ produces a steeper function and higher discriminability; a larger $\beta$ produces a shallower function and lower discriminability.

Two features of the PF carry different meanings, and keeping them apart is central to this chapter. The slope (steepness) indexes sensitivity: how sharply the probability of "different" rises as the stimulus difference grows. The location ($\alpha$) marks where the function sits along the intensity axis. In a same–different task, a location shift can reflect either a genuine change in sensitivity or a change in response criterion, so it is read with caution; the slope is the cleaner sensitivity index [@macmillan2005detection; @prins2016psychophysics]. The contrast maps directly onto signal detection theory, where slope changes signal true sensitivity changes and location shifts can signal response bias [@macmillan2005detection]. @fig-pf-location-vs-sensitivity illustrates it, and the analysis in this chapter is built on it.

Two PF-based analyses then serve distinct roles. Descriptive thresholds and slopes, estimated per participant from the behavioral data, form a behavioral backbone for the effort manipulation; the fitting procedure is detailed in @sec-pf-estimation. The primary inferential test uses a trial-level probit GLMM that models the choice on every trial, keeps the continuous intensity scale rather than binning it, and asks whether momentary arousal changes the slope rather than the criterion.

## Arousal, Effort, and Competing Mechanisms

The most direct way physical effort could disrupt concurrent cognition is resource competition. Limited-capacity and multiple-resource accounts hold that effort and cognition draw on overlapping pools, so performance falls once their combined demand exceeds capacity [@kahneman1973; @navon1984; @navon1985; @wickens2008]. Interference can come from sustaining force, from motor–cognitive competition during response selection, and from arousal that helps or harms depending on state [@proctor2012; @woollacott2002]. These costs grow with age, plausibly reflecting reduced reserve or altered executive control [@beurskens2014; @verhaeghen2003]. In one demonstration, older adults lost visual working memory accuracy while holding a 30% MVC grip, whereas younger adults were largely spared [@azer2023].

Effort can also act through arousal, by changing the internal state in which a decision is made rather than by draining a shared resource. Two frameworks shape the prediction. The Yerkes–Dodson law describes an inverted-U: performance climbs with arousal to an optimum, then declines as further arousal, often felt as stress, begins to impair it [@yerkes1908]. Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT) supplies a mechanism. Tonic (baseline) and phasic (event-evoked) LC activity set neural gain, and behavior is best when tonic activity is moderate and phasic responses to relevant events are strong [@astonjones2005].

Aging appears to move the operating point on this curve. Older adults may show a leftward shift or compression of the inverted-U, so peak performance occurs at lower objective demand than in younger adults [@mather2016; @mikneviciute2022]. A load that is neutral or even helpful for a younger adult can therefore push an older adult past the optimum, onto the descending limb where performance falls [@huang2024; @mather2016]. This is the specific vulnerability the present study probes: whether an induced arousal load degrades the quality of perceptual evidence in older adults.

Physical effort offers a controlled way to raise arousal while leaving stimulus difficulty untouched. Sustained isometric handgrip at moderate-to-high intensity (roughly 30–40% of maximum voluntary contraction, MVC) produces a reliable pressor and sympathoexcitatory response, raising arterial pressure, heart rate, and sympathetic outflow, and that response persists in older adults. Static handgrip and post-exercise ischemia also engage brainstem and cortical regions for autonomic control [@lalande2014; @mark1985; @sander2010; @toska2010]. Handgrip is therefore a useful perturbation of arousal physiology, though not a direct readout of tonic LC firing; its sympathoexcitation is only an indirect route into the LC-linked mechanisms AGT emphasizes.

Resource competition and arousal modulation are not mutually exclusive, and accuracy or mean reaction time cannot tell them apart. The present design separates them by construction. Effort condition captures the aggregate cost of the grip, which may blend both influences; trial-by-trial pupil state isolates momentary arousal; and the psychometric function tells a change in sensitivity apart from a change in criterion. A broad effort effect would fit either mechanism. A stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction, arousal tracking sensitivity from one trial to the next, would point specifically to arousal-linked modulation.

## Pupillometry as an Index of Arousal

Measuring arousal at the trial level calls for a fast, noninvasive index, and pupil diameter provides one. Pupil size covaries with arousal-related neuromodulation and is often linked to LC–NE activity [@astonjones2005; @gilzenrat2010]. It can be read at two timescales. Baseline (tonic) diameter tracks sustained arousal and general alertness [@alnaes2014pupil; @gilzenrat2010]. Task-evoked pupil responses (TEPRs), the phasic dilations that follow an event, track the momentary mobilization of effort during a decision [@beatty1982; @kahneman1966].

A TEPR typically peaks one to two seconds after stimulus onset and can be summarized by peak amplitude, mean dilation, or the area under the baseline-corrected curve (AUC), which captures both amplitude and duration. Larger TEPRs accompany harder decisions and greater cognitive load, consistent with increased recruitment of control [@kiefer2018; @preuschoff2011pupil]. The link to the LC runs through direct projections to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus, which drives pupil dilation and constriction [@joshi2016; @mcDougal2010; @murphy2014].

Pupil diameter is a multi-determined signal, so it must be read with care. Eye position, saccades, and blink-related data loss can all distort apparent size, and these artifacts are more common in older samples [@papesh2024modern; @laeng2024; @hershman2024]. Because pupil responses also lag their triggering events by roughly 200–250 ms, event-locked analysis windows are needed to isolate the response of interest [@hershman2024]. These constraints shape the present analysis in two ways: the primary test uses a phasic, stimulus-locked pupil metric paired with explicit quality control, and tonic state is addressed only indirectly, through the effort manipulation checks.

Aging changes the system being indexed. The LC degrades structurally in older adults [@mather2016], and functional compensation may follow, including chronically elevated tonic arousal or blunted phasic responses to challenge [@lee2018; @mather2016neural]. Such dynamics can support performance up to a point, but may also heighten vulnerability to supra-optimal arousal [@astonjones2005; @eldar2013]. Older samples often show larger baseline pupils alongside reduced task-evoked responses, a pattern that suggests an altered tonic–phasic balance [@granholm2007]. Physical effort offers a way to test whether an externally imposed arousal load shifts these dynamics and whether momentary pupil state tracks changes in sensitivity.

## Linking Arousal to Sensitivity: State, Trait, and the Interaction Test

Connecting pupil to behavior raises one more issue: a participant's average arousal (a trait) and their fluctuation around that average (a state) can pull in different directions, and conflating them is a known hazard in pupil–behavior work. To keep them apart, each trial's pupil metric $P_{ij}$ is split by within-subject centering into a between-person trait component and a within-person state component:

$$P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} = \overline{P}_{j}, \qquad P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} = P_{ij} - \overline{P}_{j}$$ {#eq-state-trait}

The trait component is the subject mean; the state component is the trial's deviation from it.

The decomposition lets one model answer two questions at once: whether people with higher average arousal differ in sensitivity, and whether a person discriminates differently on trials when they are more aroused than usual. Separating the two matters especially in aging, where trait differences may carry the imprint of health or cognitive reserve [@enders2013; @hoffman2015]. If high-arousal individuals perform worse for reasons unrelated to moment-to-moment change, such as a comorbidity, that pattern is absorbed at the trait level rather than misread as a within-trial arousal effect. @fig-decompose-state-trait shows the logic.

```{r decompose-state-trait}

#|   **(A)** Raw pupil problem. Baseline pupil diameter differs between people, so the same raw value can mean high arousal for one participant and low arousal for another; raw values are therefore misleading for cross-person comparisons.
#|   **(B)** Trait versus state decomposition. Each trial-level pupil metric $P_{ij}$ splits into a **trait** component, the subject mean $\overline{P}_j$, and a **state** component, the deviation from that mean, $P_{ij} - \overline{P}_j = P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$.
#|   **(C)** Inferential goal: slope modulation. The primary interaction ($X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$) tests whether moment-to-moment arousal changes the steepness (sensitivity) of the psychometric function, not only intercept or criterion.
#|   **(D)** Measurement window and model. The timeline shows squeeze onset through trial end; the shaded **Cognitive AUC** window (4.85--6.05 s from squeeze onset) captures task-evoked pupil response. The equation summarizes the probit-link GLMM used for inference (full specification in text).
#| fig-width: 10

#| out-width: "100%"
```

These pieces combine in a hierarchical probit GLMM of the trial-level choice, with continuous stimulus intensity, effort, modality, and the state and trait pupil components as predictors, and by-subject random intercepts and intensity slopes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{probit}(P(Y_{ij}=1)) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Effort}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Modality}_{ij} + \beta_4 P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} \\
&\quad + \beta_5 (X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}) + \beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} + \beta_7 (X_{ij} \times \text{Effort}_{ij}) + u_{0j} + u_{1j}X_{ij}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-primary-glmm}

The term that matters most for H3 is $\beta_5$: the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction tests whether the slope of the psychometric function, and therefore sensitivity, changes with momentary arousal. The term $\beta_7$ (stimulus intensity × effort) tests the analogous question for H1 at the trial level—whether high effort changes the slope of the function—complementing the per-participant PF comparison described in @sec-statistical-analysis. An effect confined to the intercept ($\beta_2$) would indicate a shift in response tendency without a change in sensitivity. The full specification appears in @sec-glmm.

## Research Questions and Hypotheses

The rationale above motivates four questions, each with a directional prediction.

First, does effort change the behavioral psychometric function? We compare high (40% MVC) and low (5% MVC) effort on per-participant thresholds and slopes in both tasks. We expect higher thresholds under high effort, while noting that a threshold shift can reflect sensitivity or criterion, and we predict shallower slopes, the signature of reduced discriminability under elevated arousal (H1).

Second, does high effort raise arousal as intended? Following the operationalization in Chapter 1, we distinguish two pupil-based arousal indices. H2a predicts greater sustained trial-period dilation (Total AUC, referenced to pre-squeeze B0) under high effort—a signature of overall effort-related arousal during the grip epoch. H2b predicts larger stimulus-locked task-evoked responses (Cognitive AUC, B1-corrected) under high effort—a signature of enhanced phasic event-related arousal. Pre-squeeze baseline diameter (B0) serves as a supplementary, cleaner index of resting pupil state and is analyzed alongside Total AUC to separate pre-trial tonic level from effort-induced dilation.

Third, does momentary arousal modulate sensitivity? Modeling intensity continuously, we test the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction. The primary prediction is a negative interaction, shallower slopes on higher-arousal trials, consistent with supra-optimal arousal degrading the sensory evidence; a positive interaction, indicating enhancement at moderate arousal, is the alternative. Trait-level arousal is expected to show weaker or null effects, since it may be confounded with individual differences such as cognitive reserve (H3).

Finally, do people who react more strongly to effort change more behaviorally? We test whether larger effort-evoked pupil changes (Δpupil) accompany larger changes in psychometric parameters (Δthreshold, Δslope), predicting that stronger physiological reactivity tracks larger behavioral shifts (H4).

# Methods

## Participants {#sec-participants}

Older adults (*M* = 69.1 years, *SD* = 6.0, range 60--83; 33 women, 28 men) were recruited from the LC Aging study behavioral cohort. @fig-participant-flow (@sec-data-quality) traces recruitment through psychometric and pupil-quality exclusions to the analytic streams used here; the figure should be read for the full accounting. In brief, 64 and 65 participants entered the ADT and VDT arms, and 61 contributed merged trial-level behavioral--pupil data to this chapter.

Participants were aged 60 or older, right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and adequate hearing for tone discrimination, and had no neurological, psychiatric, or cardiovascular conditions likely to affect arousal or pupil dynamics. Medications known to alter pupil diameter (e.g., anticholinergics, opioids, alpha-adrenergic agents) were exclusionary, as was inability to sustain 5% or 40% MVC grip safely. Cognitive screening used the phone-adapted Montreal Cognitive Assessment (blind MoCA), scored out of 22 rather than the in-person /30 version. MoCA and years of education were available for 57 of the 61 merged-sample participants; scores ranged from 17 to 22 (*M* = 19.8, *SD* = 1.6), above typical impairment cutoffs on the blind scale (≈17--18), and education averaged 15.9 years (*SD* = 2.6). All participants provided written informed consent under an IRB-approved protocol and were compensated per study policy.

Trial-level analyses use the merged behavioral--pupil file. The primary GLMM requires complete cognitive pupil metrics, stimulus intensity, and choice (@sec-power-analysis).

## Task Paradigm

Task overview. Participants completed two same–different discrimination tasks (an Auditory Discrimination Task [ADT] and a Visual Discrimination Task [VDT]) while maintaining concurrent isometric hand-grip on a dynamometer. On each trial, a *standard* and *probe* stimulus were presented in sequence; participants judged whether the two were the same or different, then rated their confidence. Both tasks used the same response-signal timeline and effort manipulation (@fig-paradigm).

Trial timeline and effort. Each trial began with a jittered blank interval (1.5–4.5 s) on a gray background. Participants then saw a 3 s rectangular grip gauge whose marker indicated the target force (either 5% or 40% of maximum voluntary contraction [MVC]) to be held with the left hand on a handheld dynamometer. MVC was assessed in a short calibration before each task. Participants were instructed to maintain force through the probe stimulus and to release the grip at the onset of the subsequent 0.25 s post-probe blank screen (a blue-bordered blank appearing at approximately 4.45 s from squeeze onset), roughly 400 ms before the cognitive AUC window opened. After that blank came a 3 s same/different response window, and a 3 s four-point confidence rating. From squeeze onset through the end of the confidence period, the fixed portion of the timeline lasted 10.7 s; including the pre-trial jitter and the preprocessed pre-squeeze baseline used for pupil segmentation, the full trial epoch matches the 13.7 s timeline used in the MATLAB preprocessing pipeline.

```{r paradigm-schematic}
#| label: fig-paradigm
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Experimental paradigm (response-signal design). Jittered pre-trial interval followed by a 3 s grip-gauge period (Low vs. High effort), fixation and standard–probe sequence, then 3 s same/different and 3 s confidence. Auditory and visual stimulus classes are summarized in the task sections below; timing follows the schematic.
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center

paradigm_path <- file.path(chapter2_dir, "output", "figures", "Paradigm.png")
if (file.exists(paradigm_path)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(paradigm_path)
} else {
  alt <- file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", "Paradigm.png")
  if (file.exists(alt)) {
    knitr::include_graphics(alt)
  } else {
    cat("*Figure: Paradigm.png not found. Expected at:* ", paradigm_path, "*")
  }

```

Auditory task (ADT). The standard was a 0.1 s sinusoidal tone at 1000 Hz. After a 0.5 s ISI, the probe was a 0.1 s tone identical to the standard (Δfrequency = 0) or frequency-incremented by 8, 16, 32, or 64 Hz.

Visual task (VDT). The standard was a foveal sinusoidal Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/°, Michelson contrast 0.20, diameter 4°, duration 0.1 s). The probe matched the standard (Δcontrast = 0) or increased in contrast by 0.06, 0.12, 0.24, or 0.48 with other parameters fixed.

Responses. After stimulus offset, participants released the grip and used the right hand to respond within 3 s (index finger = “different,” middle finger = “same”). A 3 s confidence screen followed (four levels, 1 = lowest to 4 = highest confidence).

Scheduling and feedback. Each task comprised 150 trials per full set (five blocks of 30), crossing the five stimulus levels (standard plus four offsets) with the two effort conditions in pseudorandom order with equal allocation (three trials per stimulus × effort combination per block when the full schedule was collected). Grip performance was reviewed between blocks; participants received corrective feedback if force was repeatedly off-target or not maintained through the probe as required. Task runs were acquired in-scanner (Session 2 and Session 3 in the study database; practice and Session 1 were excluded from analysis files). Low- and high-effort trials were intermixed within runs rather than blocked by session. Realized trial counts vary when runs were omitted (@sec-data-quality).

Stimuli were presented and responses collected using the LC Aging in-scanner setup: visual stimulation via a PROPixx-class projector (VPixx Technologies; high refresh rate, HD resolution) viewed through a head-coil mirror at approximately 12 cm effective viewing distance; auditory stimulation through MRI-compatible earphones; fiber-optic response hardware for choices; MRI-compatible dynamometer for grip force; and binocular eye tracking for pupil diameter (250 Hz in the processed data used here; see Pupillometry). Stimulus delivery and timing used Psychophysics Toolbox [@brainard1997] in MATLAB; neuroimaging results are reported elsewhere.

## Pupillometry {#sec-pupillometry}

Pupil diameter was recorded continuously throughout each trial at 250 Hz and processed using a MATLAB preprocessing pipeline that segments trials relative to squeeze onset, flags blinks and track loss events, computes window-specific validity metrics, and implements subtractive baseline correction using pre-event windows.

Metrics and preprocessing. The first derived measure was Total AUC: baseline-corrected area under the pupil curve over a global trial window (0–4.70 s from squeeze onset, B0 reference), indexing sustained arousal during the concurrent physical effort. This operationalization follows Chapter 1, in which Total AUC reliably tracked the effort manipulation across three cognitive tasks in younger adults; it is dominated by the sustained dilation produced by the handgrip and captures overall physiological state during the task rather than the phasic response to the cognitive target. The second measure, which served as the primary predictor in trial-level models, was the cognitive pupil metric: a baseline-corrected, task-evoked summary from a fixed 1.20 s stimulus-locked window spanning 4.85–6.05 s (target onset + 0.50 s through +1.70 s relative to squeeze onset, B1 reference). That window targets the TEPR peak—typically around one second after stimulus onset [@mathot2023methods]—while limiting early reflex contributions and RT-driven confounds. Chapter 1 used a shorter, probe-proximal window as an exploratory metric; the fixed peak-aligned window here is a deliberate upgrade that better captures the full TEPR. Analyses used mean dilation (AUC divided by window duration) rather than raw AUC, which removes duration confounds. Because Total AUC and Cognitive AUC reference different subtractive baselines (B0 vs. B1), effort effects on each metric were interpreted alongside direct tests of baseline diameter (@sec-manipulation-check).

Baseline correction was implemented subtractively (*pupil* - baseline mean). For Total AUC, the baseline window was the pre-squeeze interval from −0.5 s to 0.0 s relative to squeeze onset (B0 baseline). For the cognitive pupil metric, the baseline window was the pre-target interval from 3.85 s to 4.35 s relative to squeeze onset (B1 baseline). This target-proximal baseline was chosen so that the cognitive window reflects event-linked dilation relative to the immediately preceding pre-target pupil level, while the global Total AUC reflects overall dilation across the sustained effort epoch.

Quality control and confound mitigation. Gap-aware quality control metrics were developed following @kret2019preprocessing to distinguish genuine low pupil dilation from data quality artifacts arising from fragmented missing-data segments. A trial can have acceptable overall validity (e.g., 60%) yet contain a large contiguous gap that distorts AUC estimates; percentage-validity thresholds are therefore not always sufficient for quality screening. Full metric specifications are given in @sec-appendix-a, but the saved model objects reported in this chapter were fit using three pre-defined inclusion tiers (primary, lenient, and strict; see below).

### Pupil quality tiers {#sec-pupil-quality-tiers}

Pupil-based analyses used three pre-defined percentage-validity tiers from the processed dataset. The primary tier required at least 60% valid samples in both the pre-squeeze baseline window and the cognitive window; the lenient tier used a 50% threshold for both windows; the strict tier required 70% for both. An expanded B1/gap-aware screening framework was developed in parallel preprocessing documentation, but those thresholds were not the operative inclusion flags for the saved analysis objects summarized here. Accordingly, the reported results should be interpreted as reflecting the simpler percentage-validity tiers above.

Psychophysical modeling guidance emphasizes that assuming lapse rate ($\lambda$) = 0 can distort threshold and slope estimates if lapses are present but unaccounted for [@prins2016psychophysics]. This concern is particularly relevant in older adult populations, where attentional lapses, track loss events, and data quality issues may be more frequent. The quality-tier strategy addresses this by excluding trials with poorer pupil validity, thereby reducing lapse-like contamination in the psychometric function estimates. The tiering approach tests robustness of conclusions across stricter inclusion criteria: if key effects (e.g., the stimulus intensity × pupil state interaction) are consistent across lenient, primary, and strict quality tiers, this provides evidence that findings are not driven solely by the specific validity threshold used. This strategy is consistent with psychophysical best practices for handling stimulus-independent errors without explicitly estimating lapse parameters in the primary model [@prins2016psychophysics].

### Cognitive window and response-screen timing {#sec-response-timing}

The primary cognitive window (4.85–6.05 s from squeeze onset) targets the TEPR peak following the probe stimulus. The grip is released at the onset of the post-probe blank (~4.45 s), so the effort manipulation is complete approximately 400 ms before the window opens. This means the cognitive metric reflects post-release pupil state plus the task-evoked response to the discrimination target, not ongoing grip-related dilation. The window does, however, unavoidably overlap two other task events: the response screen at 4.70 s (350 ms after target onset at 4.35 s) and the button press at a variable time. In the primary GLMM sample, **RT** was measured from response-screen onset (4.70 s); median RT was `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_rt) else "—"` s overall (`r format_task_timing(response_timing, "median_rt")`), corresponding to median press times of `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_press) else "—"` s relative to squeeze onset (`r format_task_timing(response_timing, "median_press")`). These values align with the median response markers in @fig-pupil-timeseries. The analytic goal is not to eliminate the response-screen and motor confounds (which is impossible), but to limit their impact, acknowledge what remains, and support conclusions with sensitivity analyses.

Accordingly, the primary cognitive window (4.85--6.05 s) was stimulus-locked and of fixed duration, and the pupil summary was mean dilation (AUC divided by duration), which together reduce mechanical coupling of RT to AUC and duration-related artifacts relative to raw AUC. Motor-buffered and pre-response window definitions were also pre-computed (truncating the primary window 150 ms before button press, and a decision-aligned window excluding the final 150 ms before response, respectively); full AUC computation for those windows requires re-processing and is reserved for future sensitivity analyses (@sec-appendix-e). Finally, a slow-RT sensitivity subset flags trials where the button press falls after the cognitive window (RT > 1.5 s, press after 6.20 s), so motor execution cannot overlap the pupil epoch; that subset feeds the analysis in @sec-pupil-quality-tier and @sec-appendix-b.

### Sample retention and exclusions by task {#sec-sample-retention}

Participant flow was evaluated separately by modality because psychometric validity and pupil-data quality were gated independently for ADT and VDT (@sec-analytic-samples; @fig-participant-flow). Of 64 participants recruited for the auditory task, 54 entered the pupil-QC final sample (10 excluded from that stream). Of those 10, 3 had Psignifit thresholds above 64 Hz (prespecified PF invalidity) and 7 had excessive eye-track loss (greater than 50% invalid samples) or other pupil QC failures. For PF inference, only the three ADT threshold-invalid participants are excluded from the PF-valid sample (61 ADT with converged, in-range fits); pupil-QC failure does not exclude participants from PF analyses. Of 65 participants recruited for the visual task, 56 entered the pupil-QC final sample (9 excluded). None of the visual exclusions were attributed to PF threshold estimates; all nine reflected track loss or QC failures. These counts align with @fig-participant-flow (@sec-data-quality).

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-statistical-analysis}

### Analytic samples and exclusion criteria {#sec-analytic-samples}

Pupil-quality exclusions gate trial-level GLMM analyses, effort–pupil manipulation checks, and missingness diagnostics. PF-validity exclusions gate descriptive and inferential psychometric-function analyses: converged fits only, and for ADT, threshold estimates at or below the maximum tested offset (64 Hz). Pupil-QC failure has no bearing on behavioral PF inference; conversely, PF-invalid fits are excluded from PF summaries regardless of pupil data quality. The two streams therefore differ in *N* by design (@fig-participant-flow). Within the pupil-QC stream, the primary GLMM further requires complete cognitive pupil metrics and choice data, so its trial count is smaller than the primary-tier pupil-quality gate alone (@sec-data-quality). Subject-level PF–pupil coupling uses the intersection of both streams (valid PF change scores and primary-tier pupil data in both effort conditions), which is why coupling *N* is smaller than either stream alone.

### Psychometric function estimation {#sec-pf-estimation}

Behavioral data were fit in Psignifit 4 (MATLAB; @schutt2016painfree) using a beta-binomial observation model for the counts of "different" responses at each stimulus level. This choice was motivated by overdispersion: at a given intensity, empirical variability in binary outcomes can exceed the variance implied by a standard binomial model, which assumes independent Bernoulli trials with a single underlying probability. The beta-binomial formulation relaxes that assumption by introducing a dispersion metric $\eta$ (eta), estimated jointly with the psychometric function parameters. Together with threshold and slope (and asymptotic parameters), $\eta$ indexes extra-binomial variability and supports more robust parameter recovery when performance fluctuates beyond simple binomial sampling error.

Psychometric function parameters (thresholds and slopes) used as the behavioral backbone were taken from these fits. A Weibull psychometric function was fit to the proportion of "different" responses across continuous stimulus intensity levels, separately for each participant × task/modality × effort condition.

Zero-intensity replacement (Weibull compatibility). The Weibull link is undefined at a stimulus intensity of 0. Because trials with physically identical standard and probe stimuli (0-offset conditions) would otherwise require a numerical intensity of 0, a systematic replacement was applied: the 0-offset level was coded as half of the smallest non-zero stimulus level tested in each modality (the same anchor convention used to generate the descriptive psychometric summaries in @tbl-pf-params). For the auditory task, the smallest non-zero frequency offset was 8 Hz, so the 0-offset condition was assigned 4 Hz. For the visual task, the 0-offset condition was assigned 0.0075 Michelson contrast units. This procedure retains the full range of difficulty levels (including the physically identical pair) while ensuring mathematical compatibility with the Psignifit 4 fitting engine. This convention was adopted from the in-preparation behavioral report describing the same cohort; using the same anchor ensures that threshold estimates are on a comparable scale across analyses.

Limitations of the anchor choice. Replacing 0 with half of the smallest non-zero level is a conventional but somewhat arbitrary choice. A smaller anchor would place the 0-offset condition closer to 0 on the fitted curve, pulling the estimated guess rate γ higher; a larger anchor would compress the lower asymptote region. Both alternatives would affect absolute threshold estimates but not the relative comparison between effort conditions, because the same anchor is applied identically across High and Low effort and across participants. The practical leverage of the anchor on slope is also limited: for participants whose psychometric function is well-constrained, the threshold falls well above the replacement value (roughly in the mid-range of the tested levels), so the 0-offset data point mainly anchors the lower asymptote rather than shaping the rising portion of the curve where slope is estimated. Participants for whom the threshold estimate falls near or below the replacement value are flagged as PF-invalid and excluded from inferential analyses, providing a second guard against anchor-induced distortion. For the trial-level GLMM, no replacement is applied: intensity values enter the model as recorded (including 0 for same trials), and standardization within task maps the full integer range to a common scale. The zero-anchor concern therefore applies only to the Psignifit PF fits, and principally to the interpretation of the lower asymptote and absolute threshold units, not to the primary inferential test.

Guess and lapse parameters were allowed to vary freely during fitting (i.e., $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ were free parameters), consistent with psychophysical guidance that fixing lapse at zero can bias threshold and slope estimates when lapses are present [@prins2016psychophysics; @wichmann2001psychometric].

A practical concern with five-parameter Psignifit fits over five intensity levels per cell is that slope estimates can be weakly constrained, particularly for participants whose data are noisy or sparse. Three features of the fitting procedure partially address this. First, the beta-binomial dispersion parameter $\eta$ absorbs over-binomial variability that would otherwise distort threshold and slope recovery. Second, Psignifit 4's Bayesian engine applies regularizing priors over all parameters, which stabilizes estimates when the data are not fully informative. Third, and most importantly, the per-participant Weibull fits serve as a descriptive behavioral backbone—they describe average discrimination performance per condition and motivate the trial-level GLMM—but the primary inferential claims about arousal–sensitivity coupling rest on the GLMM, not the PF fits. The fitting approach and exclusion criteria (threshold validity, in-range fits) follow the same conventions used in the in-preparation behavioral report on this cohort, which provides additional justification for these choices in the context of this specific paradigm and sample.

Threshold and slope (effective midpoint). Reported thresholds and slopes were defined at the psychometric function’s effective midpoint: the operating point located halfway between the guess rate $\gamma$ (lower asymptote) and the upper asymptote $1-\lambda$. The response probability at that midpoint is therefore
$$
\text{Threshold} = \gamma + \frac{(1 - \lambda) - \gamma}{2}.
$$
The left-hand side denotes this midpoint response probability (on the [0, 1] scale). The psychometric threshold values used in subsequent analyses are the stimulus intensities $x$ at which the fitted Weibull attains that probability (i.e., the intensity solving $\Psi(x) = \gamma + \frac{(1-\lambda)-\gamma}{2}$ for the fitted psychometric function $\Psi$). Slope was evaluated at that same effective midpoint (local steepness of $\Psi$ with respect to stimulus intensity at the threshold stimulus). In substantive terms, this stimulus-level definition indexes the intensity at which the probability of a "different" response is approximately 0.5 on an effective scale that adjusts for individual guess and lapse rates (namely, halfway between $\gamma$ and $1-\lambda$ rather than halfway between 0 and 1). This convention yields a criterion comparable to a 50% point on the effective response scale while remaining robust to variation in $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ across participants and conditions.

### Trial-level GLMM (primary model) {#sec-glmm}

The primary model used a probit link function to link phasic arousal to psychometric sensitivity:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{probit}(P(Y_{ij}=1)) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Effort}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Modality}_{ij} + \beta_4 P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} \\
&\quad + \beta_5 (X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}) + \beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} + \beta_7 (X_{ij} \times \text{Effort}_{ij}) + u_{0j} + u_{1j}X_{ij}
\end{aligned}
$$


where $Y_{ij}$ is the binary choice on trial $i$ for subject $j$, $X_{ij}$ is continuous stimulus intensity, $P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$ is the within-subject centered pupil metric (mean dilation, trial value − subject mean), and $P^{(\text{trait})}_{j}$ is the between-subject pupil metric (subject mean). The primary coupling term $X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$ ($\beta_5$) tests whether within-person fluctuations in arousal are associated with changes in psychometric sensitivity. The term $X_{ij} \times \text{Effort}_{ij}$ ($\beta_7$) tests whether effort modulates the slope of the psychometric function at the trial level, providing a direct within-subjects complement to the per-participant PF comparison for H1. The term $\beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j}$ tests whether between-subject differences in average arousal relate to sensitivity. The random effects $u_{0j}$ and $u_{1j}$ allow each participant to have their own baseline performance level and intensity sensitivity, respectively.

For model fitting, stimulus intensity was standardized within task, and the pupil state and trait components were z-scored across retained trials before estimation, so fixed-effect coefficients are interpretable on a standardized latent scale. The probit link was chosen for consistency with signal-detection-style latent evidence formulations. Probit coefficients lie on a standard-normal latent scale (variance = 1), so conventional standardized effect-size benchmarks apply directly; logistic coefficients would require rescaling by $\pi/\sqrt{3}$ to map to the same scale [@chinn2000]. For response probabilities in the present range, probit and logit links would be expected to yield qualitatively similar conclusions. The reported model includes random intercepts and by-subject slopes for stimulus intensity. Exploratory refits that additionally allowed by-subject random slopes for effort and pupil state produced singular fits; those extended specifications were not used for primary inference (see Results).

### Same–different task and probit link {#sec-probit-sdt}

In standard SDT, two models are used for same–different tasks: the differencing model (DIFF) and the independent observations model (IO). Under the DIFF model, the observer computes a signed difference between the two internal representations and responds "different" if that difference exceeds a symmetric criterion $\pm k$:

$$
P(\text{"different"} \mid \Delta) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta - k}{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}\right) + \Phi\!\left(\frac{-\Delta - k}{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}\right)
$$ {#eq-diff-sdt}

where $\Delta$ is the physical stimulus difference, $\sigma$ is internal-noise standard deviation, and $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. When the false-alarm rate (at $\Delta = 0$) is low—that is, $\Phi(-k/\sqrt{2}\sigma)$ is small—the second term in @eq-diff-sdt is negligible, and the expression reduces to $\Phi\!\left((\Delta - k)/(\sqrt{2}\sigma)\right)$, which is exactly a probit function of $\Delta$. The probit GLMM is therefore the correct functional form for this task structure in the practical operating range. At the trial level, fitting a full two-parameter SDT model (separate $d'$ and criterion per trial) is not feasible without multiple observations at each intensity per trial; the slope of the probit GLMM captures psychometric steepness (sensitivity) and the intercept captures response tendency (criterion), which is the maximum resolution the design allows.

The IO model, which predicts $P(\text{"different"}) = \Phi(d'/2 - c) + \Phi(-d'/2 - c)$, is non-monotone at very negative criteria but converges numerically with the DIFF probit form over the response-probability range in these data. Neither model provides stronger inferential leverage than the probit GLMM here. The probit specification is the appropriate choice.

### Subject-level coupling analyses {#sec-subject-coupling-methods}

Subject-level coupling tested whether participants with larger effort-evoked pupil changes also showed larger effort-evoked shifts in psychometric parameters (H4). For each participant × task, effort change scores were computed as High − Low for Cognitive AUC, Total AUC, PF threshold, and PF slope. Pearson correlations (with 95% confidence intervals) linked each Δpupil metric to each ΔPF parameter separately within ADT and VDT, yielding eight tests per modality. Analyses required valid PF change scores and primary-tier pupil data in both effort conditions (@sec-analytic-samples). Influence diagnostics (Cook's distance, leverage, DFBETAS) flagged outlier-sensitive correlations; Spearman ρ and correlations after excluding flagged participants served as sensitivity checks (@sec-subject-coupling, @sec-appendix-d).

### Sensitivity analyses, power, and multiplicity {#sec-sensitivity-analyses}

Trial-level analyses use all available older-adult participants and trials in the LC Aging behavioral–pupil database after preprocessing (see @sec-participants and @sec-data-quality); the sample was not sized *de novo* for the continuous-intensity GLMM reported here. The study was designed as a multimodal protocol in which these tasks were embedded alongside imaging and other measures, so the effective *N* reflects recruitment and retention in that broader study. Prospective power for the pupil × intensity interaction was therefore limited *a priori*. A sensitivity power analysis was conducted to estimate the minimum detectable effect size (MDE) given the final sample and design; results appear in @sec-power-analysis alongside the equivalence bounds.

Several pre-specified checks supported interpretation of the primary GLMM. Quality-tier robustness re-fit the model under the lenient tier (more permissive validity: pre-squeeze baseline and cognitive-window validity each $\geq$ 0.50) and the strict tier (stricter: each $\geq$ 0.70), in addition to the primary tier (both $\geq$ 0.60), to assess whether inferences about the stimulus intensity × pupil state interaction depended on inclusion stringency. A slow-RT subset restricted analysis to trials with button press after the cognitive window (RT > 1.5 s), to limit motor overlap with the pupil epoch (@sec-response-timing). Model comparison contrasted the primary model with a nested model omitting the interaction, using Akaike’s information criterion (AIC), where a meaningful improvement (e.g., $\Delta$AIC > 2) would favor retaining the interaction. Missingness diagnostics tested whether pupil loss related to effort, intensity, task, or RT (@sec-missingness; quality-tier robustness in @sec-pupil-quality-tier; supplementary tables in @sec-appendix-b). Finally, equivalence testing (two one-sided tests; @lakens2017) evaluated the interaction against a pre-specified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) on the probit scale; the bound rationale is given in @sec-sesoi-rationale, and test intervals and outcome are summarized in @sec-pupil-quality-tier.

The prospectus-defined confirmatory targets were effort effects on psychometric parameters (RQ1), the effort–pupil manipulation check (RQ2), trial-level pupil–psychometric coupling (RQ3), and subject-level PF–pupil coupling (RQ4). Pre-specified sensitivity analyses (quality tiers, model comparison, slow-RT subset, equivalence) were used to stress-test those inferences, not to add new hypotheses. Exploratory analyses would have been any post-hoc tests outside the prospectus; none were run beyond what is reported, and all reported statistics correspond to the pre-registered plan.

Multiple comparisons. The analysis family spans four distinct research questions with multiple tests in each. RQ1 (effort effects on PF) yields four comparisons: threshold and slope under High vs. Low effort, separately for ADT and VDT. RQ2 (manipulation check) tests four pupil metrics—Total AUC, Cognitive AUC, B0, and B1—against effort. RQ3–RQ4 (coupling) include the primary intensity × pupil-state interaction, the effort × intensity interaction ($\beta_7$), three equivalence tests, and four subject-level PF–pupil correlations. With this many tests, family-wise error inflates without correction. We do not apply a blanket cross-RQ correction, because each research question addresses a distinct hypothesis with a separate prediction; pooling conceptually independent families would be over-conservative. Within families, Holm correction is applied to the four RQ1 comparisons (threshold and slope × ADT and VDT) and to the four RQ2 pupil-metric tests. The two interaction terms in RQ3 ($\beta_5$ and $\beta_7$) address different hypotheses (H3 vs. H1b) and are not corrected jointly. Results reported without explicit correction are described as such and should be read as suggestive rather than confirmatory. The chapter's single confirmatory conclusion rests on the primary coupling test ($\beta_5$, @eq-primary-glmm) and the equivalence result at the pre-specified SESOI.

### Software and reproducibility {#sec-software-reproducibility}

All GLMMs were estimated using the lme4 package [@bates2015] in R [@R]. Models were fit using lme4's default optimizer settings for primary and tiered analyses; the slow-RT sensitivity refit used the bobyqa optimizer with an increased maximum function-evaluation limit (200,000) to stabilize optimization with the reduced trial count. Convergence was assessed by inspecting gradient norms, optimizer warnings, and singular-fit diagnostics. Parameter estimates and standard errors were extracted using the broom.mixed package [@bolker2026broommixed]; *p*-values are based on the normal approximation to the *z*-distribution, which is appropriate for large trial-level sample sizes. 95% confidence intervals for fixed effects were computed using the Wald method. Within-subject PF effort models used lmerTest [@kuznetsova2017lmerTest] when Satterthwaite *df* were required.

Preprocessing, statistical analysis, visualization, and reporting used R [@R] with the tidyverse [@wickham2019tidyverse] and companion packages: dplyr [@dplyr], tidyr [@tidyr], readr [@readr], stringr [@stringr], purrr [@purrr], glue [@glue], ggplot2 [@wickham2016ggplot2], patchwork [@pedersen2025patchwork], ggtext [@wilke2022ggtext], GGally [@schloerke2025ggally], mgcv [@wood2011mgcv], gt [@gt], knitr [@xie2025knitr], kableExtra [@zhu2024kableextra], here [@muller2025here], data.table [@barrett2026datatable], and yaml [@stephens2025yaml]. Descriptive psychometric functions were fit in MATLAB with Psignifit 4 [@schutt2016painfree]; stimuli were presented with Psychophysics Toolbox [@brainard1997]. This chapter was authored in Quarto [@quarto].

Data and code availability. All analysis code and de-identified data are available in the project GitHub repository: `https://github.com/mohdasti/Psychometrics_Pupillometry`. A versioned archive of the analysis code and data is also available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21215384.

# Results

Results below follow the pre-registered pipeline: psychometric parameters, effort–pupil manipulation checks, missingness, trial-level coupling, subject-level coupling, and a hypothesis summary. Unless noted otherwise, models use the primary pupil-quality tier (baseline and cognitive window validity $\geq$ 0.60).

```{r data-quality-summary}
    "After applying the primary pupil-quality tier (@sec-pupil-quality-tiers), ",
    format(nt_adt_q, big.mark = ","), " ADT trials and ",
    format(nt_vdt_q, big.mark = ","), " VDT trials (",
    format(nt_total_q, big.mark = ","), " total) met the quality gate. ",
    "The primary GLMM further required non-missing cognitive pupil state, stimulus intensity, and choice, ",
    "yielding ", format(glmm_primary_sample$n_trials, big.mark = ","),
    " complete-case trials from ", glmm_primary_sample$n_sub,
    " participants (mean ", sprintf("%.1f", glmm_primary_sample$mean_trials_per_sub),
    " trials per participant). ",
    if (!is.na(n_dropped_sub) && n_dropped_sub > 0L) {
      paste0(
        "Complete-case filtering excluded ", n_dropped_sub,
        " of ", n_merged_sub,
        " participants with merged trial-level data who had no usable trials under those criteria. "
      )
    } else {
      ""
    },
    "Post-hoc power (@sec-power-analysis) uses this GLMM sample, ",
    "not the full primary-tier trial count.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*Primary-tier and GLMM sample counts could not be computed (merged data unavailable in this render). Final N is fixed in @fig-participant-flow.*\n\n")
}
```

## Behavioral Backbone (PF Outcomes) {#sec-pf-backbone}

Descriptive psychometric-function parameters for each modality and effort condition are reported in @tbl-pf-params (@sec-appendix-f); the effort contrasts that test H1 are in @tbl-pf-effort-test below.

```{r tbl-pf-effort-test}
#| label: tbl-pf-effort-test
#| tbl-cap: "Within-Subject Tests of Effort on PF Threshold and Slope (High − Low). PF-valid sample: converged fits; ADT thresholds ≤ 64 Hz."

library(lme4)

if (!is.null(pf_params)) {
  pf_h1_infer <- bind_rows(
    lapply(c("ADT", "VDT"), function(tsk) {
      bind_rows(
        lapply(c("threshold", "slope"), function(out) {
          extract_pf_effort_lmer(pf_params, tsk, out)
        })
      )
    })
  )
  if (nrow(pf_h1_infer) > 0) {
    pf_h1_infer %>%
      mutate(
        `Est. (High − Low)` = round(`Est. (High − Low)`, 3),
        SE = round(SE, 3),
        t = round(t, 3),
        df = round(df, 2),
        p = round(p, 4),
        N = n_sub
      ) %>%
      select(-n_sub) %>%
      make_table(
        col.names = c(
          "Task", "PF Parameter", "Est. (High − Low)", "SE", "t", "df", "p", "N"
        ),
        digits = 3
      )
  } else {
    cat("*Could not fit PF effort models (insufficient data).*")
    pf_h1_infer <- tibble()
  }
} else {
  cat("*PF parameters not available for inferential tests.*")
  pf_h1_infer <- tibble()
}
```

```{r pf-h1-interpret, results = "asis"}
#| echo: false

format_p_inline <- function(p) {
  if (length(p) == 0L || is.na(p)) return("\u2014")
  if (p < 0.001) return("< .001")
  sprintf("%.3f", p)
}

if (exists("pf_h1_infer") && !is.null(pf_h1_infer) && nrow(pf_h1_infer) == 4) {
  getr <- function(tsk, par) {
    pf_h1_infer %>% dplyr::filter(Task == tsk, `PF Parameter` == par) %>% dplyr::slice(1)
  }
  adt_th <- getr("ADT", "Threshold"); adt_sl <- getr("ADT", "Slope")
  vdt_th <- getr("VDT", "Threshold"); vdt_sl <- getr("VDT", "Slope")
  eff_col <- "Est. (High \u2212 Low)"

  adt_slope_sd <- filter_pf_analysis(pf_params) %>%
    dplyr::filter(task == "ADT") %>%
    dplyr::pull(slope) %>%
    stats::sd(na.rm = TRUE)

  cat(
    "@tbl-pf-effort-test reports the within-subject High \u2212 Low effort contrasts. ",
    "The auditory threshold rose under high effort (est = ", sprintf("%.2f", adt_th[[eff_col]]),
    " Hz, *t*(", round(adt_th$df, 0), ") = ", sprintf("%.2f", adt_th$t), ", *p* = ", format_p_inline(adt_th$p),
    "), the only contrast to reach significance and the basis for **partial support** of H1a; the visual threshold did not move (*p* = ",
    format_p_inline(vdt_th$p),
    "). Because several confirmatory tests were evaluated across H1 and H2, this isolated effect is best read as suggestive rather than decisive. ",
    "H1b predicted shallower slopes under high effort. Slopes were numerically shallower in both modalities but reliable in neither ",
    "(ADT *p* = ", format_p_inline(adt_sl$p), "; VDT *p* = ", format_p_inline(vdt_sl$p), "), so H1b was **not supported** by the per-participant PF analysis. ",
    "The slope null held across both tasks, and auditory slopes varied widely across participants (SD = ", sprintf("%.3f", adt_slope_sd),
    "), so it does not stem from compressed or floor-limited estimates. ",
    "The trial-level effort × intensity interaction ($\\beta_7$) from the GLMM provides a complementary and more statistically powerful test of the same question (below). ",
    "On balance, the grip manipulation behaved as a physiological stressor that nudged the auditory threshold without reliably flattening either psychometric function. ",
    "That shift is more consistent with a change in response criterion or task difficulty than with a genuine loss of sensitivity, for which the slope is the cleaner index.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*Inferential tests for PF effort effects not available.*\n\n")
}
```

```{r trial-level-effort-intensity, results = "asis"}
#| echo: false

# Trial-level effort × intensity: direct test of whether effort changes
# the slope of the psychometric function (β7 from eq-primary-glmm).

if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_effort_intensity)) {
  ei_row <- pupil_psychometric_effort_intensity %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "stimulus_intensity_scaled:effort_factorHigh")
  ef_row <- pupil_psychometric_effort_intensity %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "effort_factorHigh")
  if (nrow(ei_row) == 1L) {
    b   <- sprintf("%+.3f", ei_row$estimate)
    se  <- sprintf("%.3f", ei_row$std.error)
    z   <- sprintf("%.2f", ei_row$statistic)
    p   <- format_p_inline(ei_row$p.value)
    cat(
      "Trial-level effort \u00d7 intensity interaction ($\\beta_7$). ",
      "The stimulus intensity \u00d7 effort interaction in the expanded GLMM was $\\beta_7$ = ", b,
      " (*SE* = ", se, ", *z* = ", z, ", *p* = ", p, "). ",
      if (ei_row$p.value < .05) {
        paste0("This is significant, indicating that effort changed the steepness of the psychometric function at the trial level\u2014a direct sensitivity shift, not merely an intercept change. ")
      } else {
        paste0("This was not significant. The null trial-level slope change converges with the per-participant PF analysis (H1b not supported) and is consistent with the overall picture: the effort manipulation shifted response tendency (intercept) rather than discrimination sensitivity (slope). ")
      },
      if (nrow(ef_row) == 1L) {
        paste0(
          "The effort main effect remained negative ($\\beta_2$ = ", sprintf("%+.3f", ef_row$estimate),
          ", *SE* = ", sprintf("%.3f", ef_row$std.error),
          ", *p* = ", format_p_inline(ef_row$p.value),
          "), consistent with the primary-model result. "
        )
      } else { "" },
      "\n\n", sep = ""
    )
  } else {
    cat("*Trial-level effort \u00d7 intensity term not available in saved results.*\n\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("*Effort \u00d7 intensity model results not available; run* `04_pupil_psychometric_coupling/06_pupil_psychometric_coupling.R` *to generate.*\n\n")
}
```

## Effort–Pupil Manipulation Check {#sec-manipulation-check}

@fig-pupil-timeseries shows empirical group-mean pupil waveforms from the preprocessing pipeline: baseline-corrected isolated pupil (arbitrary units) with GAM-smoothed 95% CI bands (winsorized subject-level means), time-locked to squeeze onset, separately for ADT and VDT. Lines correspond to the factorial combination of stimulus difficulty (Easy vs. Hard) and handgrip effort (High vs. Low). Vertical markers indicate squeeze onset, standard and target onsets, and median response time (task-specific subtitles). Horizontal bars mark the pre-trial baseline (B0), the Total AUC window (0--4.70 s), the pre-stimulus baseline (B1), and the cognitive AUC window (4.85--6.05 s). These plots are observed data rather than the parametric schematic used in earlier drafts.

```{r pupil-timeseries-fig}
#| label: fig-pupil-timeseries
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Full-trial pupil waveforms (empirical group means). Baseline-corrected isolated pupil diameter
#|   (arbitrary units; GAM 95% CI on winsorized subject means) as a function of time relative to squeeze onset,
#|   for ADT (top) and VDT (bottom).
#|   Colored lines cross Easy vs. Hard stimulus difficulty with High vs. Low grip effort.
#|   Vertical dashed lines mark squeeze onset, standard (S1) and target (S2/probe) onsets, and median response onset.
#|   Grey and colored bars show B0, Total AUC (0--4.70 s), B1, and cognitive AUC (4.85--6.05 s).
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

waveform_path <- file.path(chapter2_dir, "output", "figures", "waveform.png")
if (file.exists(waveform_path)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(waveform_path)
} else {
  cat("*Figure: waveform.png not found. Expected at:* ", waveform_path, "*")
}
```

As predicted, high-effort handgrip significantly increased overall trial-period arousal (Total AUC: $\beta = 0.857$, $SE = 0.376$, $t = 2.282$, $p = .023$), but significantly attenuated task-evoked responses (Cognitive AUC: $\beta = -0.012$, $SE = 0.003$, $t = -3.859$, $p < .001$). Total AUC indexes overall arousal during the sustained squeeze epoch; Cognitive AUC is the stimulus-locked task-evoked response in the discrimination window. Mixed-effects models tested whether effort condition predicted pupil metrics (Total AUC and Cognitive AUC) while controlling for task modality.

```{r baseline-decomposition, results = "asis"}
#| echo: false

if (!is.null(baseline_effort_effects)) {
  b0 <- get_baseline_effort_row(baseline_effort_effects, "baseline_B0_mean")
  b1 <- get_baseline_effort_row(baseline_effort_effects, "baseline_b0_mean")

  cat(
    "Because the two metrics use different subtractive baselines, the dissociation must be read against raw baseline levels rather than inferred from the AUC signs alone. ",
    "Pre-squeeze baseline diameter (B0; the reference for Total AUC) did **not** differ by effort condition ",
    "(High \u2212 Low: ",
    if (!is.null(b0)) format_beta_manuscript(b0$estimate) else "\u2014",
    ", *SE* = ",
    if (!is.null(b0)) sprintf("%.3f", b0$std.error) else "\u2014",
    ", *t* = ",
    if (!is.null(b0)) sprintf("%.2f", b0$statistic) else "\u2014",
    ", *p* ",
    if (!is.null(b0)) format_p_manuscript(b0$p.value) else "\u2014",
    "). ",
    "Accordingly, the Total AUC increase reflects greater sustained dilation during the grip epoch itself, not a pre-trial baseline shift. ",
    "By contrast, pre-target baseline diameter (B1; the reference subtracted before the cognitive window) **was** elevated under High effort ",
    "(High \u2212 Low: ",
    if (!is.null(b1)) format_beta_manuscript(b1$estimate) else "\u2014",
    ", *SE* = ",
    if (!is.null(b1)) sprintf("%.3f", b1$std.error) else "\u2014",
    ", *t* = ",
    if (!is.null(b1)) sprintf("%.2f", b1$statistic) else "\u2014",
    ", *p* ",
    if (!is.null(b1)) format_p_manuscript(b1$p.value) else "\u2014",
    "). ",
    "Because Cognitive AUC is computed on B1-corrected waveforms, this elevation mechanically lowers the cognitive metric even when raw pupil diameter in the cognitive window is unchanged. ",
    "The observed Cognitive AUC reduction is therefore **partly** a baseline-correction artifact, although it is not fully explained by B1 elevation alone: @fig-pupil-timeseries shows that High-effort waveforms remain elevated through the pre-target interval, yet the cognitive-window increment above that elevated level is smaller than under Low effort. ",
    "A hard iris-ceiling account was also not supported: High-effort trials were not disproportionately concentrated in the upper tail of the Cognitive AUC distribution. ",
    "Taken together, the dissociation reflects both genuine sustained effort-related dilation (Total AUC) and metric-specific baseline choice (B1-corrected Cognitive AUC), rather than a uniform tonic increase followed by uniform phasic suppression.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*Baseline decomposition unavailable (merged data not loaded in this render).*\\n\\n")
}
```

A note on metric choice. Total AUC is referenced to B0 (pre-squeeze, −0.5 to 0 s relative to squeeze onset), and B0 did not differ between effort conditions ($p$ = .705). The Total AUC increase under High effort therefore captures genuine sustained dilation that builds during the grip itself, not a carry-over from the inter-trial interval. Cognitive AUC, on the other hand, is referenced to B1 (pre-target, 3.85–4.35 s), and B1 was elevated under High effort ($\beta$ = +0.336, $p$ = .007). Subtractive baseline correction means that any rise in B1 mechanically reduces the apparent Cognitive AUC even if raw pupil level in the cognitive window is unchanged. For this reason, the two metrics are best thought of as capturing different windows with different baselines rather than as pure tonic and phasic readouts. Total AUC is the primary index of sustained effort-related arousal—a usage consistent with Chapter 1 and with the role it played in confirming the grip manipulation across tasks. Cognitive AUC isolates the incremental task-evoked response above the elevated pre-target level, with the caveat that the B1 elevation introduces a baseline-correction asymmetry that partially drives the observed metric dissociation.

H2a predicted greater sustained trial-period arousal (Total AUC) under High effort, and the data support that pattern—Total AUC rose significantly ($\beta = 0.857$, $p = .023$) while pre-squeeze B0 did not differ ($p = .705$), so the increase built during the grip epoch rather than carrying over from the inter-trial interval. H2b predicted larger task-evoked responses (Cognitive AUC) under High effort; that prediction was not supported. Cognitive AUC fell ($\beta = -0.012$, $p < .001$). The metrics moved in opposite directions: Total AUC, referenced to stable B0, tracks sustained dilation during the squeeze, whereas Cognitive AUC subtracts a B1 baseline that itself rose with effort—partly compressing the corrected value. The waveforms in @fig-pupil-timeseries nonetheless suggest some genuine attenuation of the incremental response above the elevated pre-target level.

The opposite signs of these two effects are the central result of the manipulation check. @fig-effort-dissociation places the effort effect on each metric on a common axis: overall arousal rises while the task-evoked response falls. Participant-level means for each metric are shown in @sec-appendix-b (@fig-effort-pupil).

```{r fig-effort-dissociation}
#|   effort (High vs. Low) effect expressed as a t statistic; the shaded band marks the non-significant
#|   region (|t| < 1.96). Total AUC (overall trial arousal) increases under high effort while Cognitive
#|   AUC (the stimulus-locked task-evoked response) decreases, so the two effects fall on opposite sides

}
```

## Missingness Diagnostic {#sec-missingness}

Missingness was significantly predicted by effort condition (OR = 1.203, *z* = 3.672, *p* < .001) and task modality (OR = 1.967, *z* = 12.584, *p* < .001), but not by stimulus intensity (*p* = .565) or response time (*p* = .982). High-effort trials were approximately 20% more likely to yield usable pupil data than Low-effort trials, possibly reflecting reduced blinking during the more demanding squeeze. VDT trials had nearly twice the odds of retaining usable data relative to ADT trials. Missingness is not predicted by stimulus intensity or response time, suggesting that within-retained trials the psychometric intensity range and decision difficulty are not systematically distorted. Nevertheless, the non-random missingness by effort and task means that analysis samples differ systematically across conditions, which is a genuine selection-bias limitation (see @sec-missingness-limitation). Full model output and the RT-by-availability figure are in @sec-appendix-c.

## Pupil–Psychometric Coupling (Primary Analysis) {#sec-coupling-primary}

```{r primary-coupling}
#| label: tbl-pupil-psychometric
#| tbl-cap: "Primary GLMM: Pupil–Psychometric Coupling"

if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_effects)) {
  library(lme4)
  tbl <- pupil_psychometric_effects %>%
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value)

  mod_primary_path <- file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_primary.rds")
  if (file.exists(mod_primary_path)) {
    mod_primary <- readRDS(mod_primary_path)
    ci_wald <- confint(mod_primary, method = "Wald", parm = "beta_")
    ci_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
      term = rownames(ci_wald),
      `95% CI Lower` = ci_wald[, 1L],
      `95% CI Upper` = ci_wald[, 2L]
    )
    tbl <- dplyr::left_join(tbl, ci_tbl, by = "term")
  } else {
    tbl <- tbl %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        `95% CI Lower` = estimate - stats::qnorm(0.975) * std.error,
        `95% CI Upper` = estimate + stats::qnorm(0.975) * std.error
      )
  }

  term_labels <- c(
    "(Intercept)"                                              = "Intercept",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled"                                = "Stimulus Intensity",
    "pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil State (within-person)",
    "effort_factorHigh"                                        = "Effort: High vs. Low",
    "task_factorVDT"                                           = "Task: VDT vs. ADT",
    "pupil_cognitive_trait_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil Trait (between-person)",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled:pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"   = "Stimulus Intensity × Pupil State",
    "rt_scaled"                                                = "Reaction Time (covariate)"
  )

  tbl <- tbl %>%
    dplyr::mutate(term = dplyr::recode(term, !!!term_labels)) %>%
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, `95% CI Lower`, `95% CI Upper`, std.error, statistic, p.value)

  make_table(
    tbl,
    col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper", "SE", "z", "p"),
    digits = 4
  )
} else {
  cat("*Primary coupling analysis results not yet available.*")
}
```

Hypothesis 3a predicted a negative intensity × pupil-state interaction—shallower psychometric slopes on high-arousal trials if supra-optimal arousal degrades sensitivity. At the primary tier the interaction was not significant ($\beta = 0.035$, $p = .245$; @tbl-pupil-psychometric). The estimate was positive ($\mathrm{SE} = 0.030$, 95% Wald CI $[-0.024,\, +0.095]$), but the slow-RT subset reversed sign ($\beta = -0.071$), so the direction of any true coupling is indeterminate. High effort reduced overall "different" responding ($\beta = -0.139$, $z = -3.023$, $p = .003$)—a response-tendency shift rather than a demonstrated sensitivity loss. Pupil state as a main effect approached significance ($\beta = -0.046$, $p = .056$); pupil trait did not ($\beta = -0.052$, $p = .565$; H3c). Limited precision, a fixed cognitive window that may miss the arousal dynamics most relevant to choice, or genuinely weak coupling could all underlie the null; the pre-specified checks below narrow that reading.

Model-predicted psychometric functions at low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD) pupil state are shown in @sec-appendix-b (@fig-appendix-b1-predicted). Apparent separation between curves reflects extrapolation across the full scaled intensity range and should not be read as evidence for coupling given the null primary interaction (@tbl-pupil-psychometric). Exploratory binned functions by pupil tertile (@fig-appendix-b2-tertiles, @sec-appendix-b) are descriptive only and can overstate coupling when the GLMM interaction is null.

### Robustness checks: quality tiers and equivalence (TOST) {#sec-pupil-quality-tier}

The stimulus intensity $\times$ pupil state interaction was significant only in the lenient quality tier ($\beta = +0.064$, $SE = 0.028$, $z = 2.30$, $p = .021$), but did not persist in the primary tier ($\beta = +0.035$, $SE = 0.030$, $z = 1.163$, $p = .245$) or the strict tier ($\beta = +0.039$, $SE = 0.032$, $z = 1.213$, $p = .225$). This inconsistency across quality tiers indicates the effect is **not robust**: the lenient tier includes trials with lower data quality, and the lenient-tier significance likely reflects greater statistical power from the larger trial count rather than a consistent signal. AIC comparison showed the model without the interaction term fit marginally better (Without: 4187.47; With: 4188.13; $\Delta$AIC = 0.66), consistent with the non-significant interaction coefficient. Supplementary tier-wise output and AIC tables appear in @sec-appendix-b.

The slow-RT sensitivity subset (trials with RT > 1.5 s, *N* = 940 trials from 52 participants) yielded $\beta$ = −0.071, *SE* = 0.051, *z* = −1.39, *p* = .164, opposite in sign to the primary-tier estimate. This sign reversal means motor contamination of the cognitive pupil window cannot be excluded as a partial contributor to the primary-tier pattern, though neither analysis supports a reliable interaction. Across these sensitivity checks, there is no robust evidence for moment-to-moment pupil state modulating psychometric sensitivity at the primary analysis level.

Equivalence was tested with two one-sided tests (TOST) using a pre-specified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of $\pm 0.10$ probit units (full rationale in @sec-sesoi-rationale). @fig-equivalence-forest summarizes the interaction across quality tiers and the slow-RT subset (per-subset TOST values appear in @tbl-tost-equivalence, @sec-appendix-b). At the primary tier, the 90% confidence interval for the interaction ($\mathrm{LB} = -0.015$, $\mathrm{UB} = +0.085$) fell entirely within the equivalence bounds. Both one-sided TOST tests were significant at the primary tier (lower: $z = 4.50$, $p < .001$; upper: $z = -2.17$, $p = .015$), so the data are consistent with equivalence to zero at this SESOI for the primary analysis: coupling effects larger in magnitude than $\pm 0.10$ probit units are statistically incompatible with the primary-tier estimate. By contrast, the lenient tier 90% CI extended to +0.110 (upper bound exceeds the SESOI), and the slow-RT subset interval crossed zero with opposite sign ($\beta = -0.071$), so equivalence was **not supported** in those sensitivity analyses. The frequentist null hypothesis ($\beta = 0$) was not rejected at $\alpha = .05$ in the primary tier, but the equivalence framing implies that any non-null coupling, if present, is negligible relative to the SESOI rather than that the study was simply underpowered to detect the point estimate.

```{r fig-equivalence-forest}

#| fig-cap: >
#|   TOST equivalence for the stimulus intensity x pupil-state interaction across analysis subsets.
#|   Points show probit-scale interaction estimates with 90% confidence intervals; the shaded band marks the pre-specified SESOI (+/-0.10 probit units). Point color indicates the TOST equivalence verdict; trial and participant counts and Wald *p* values appear at right.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-align: center

eq_png <- fig_path("fig_equivalence_forest.png", return_absolute = TRUE)
if (!is.null(eq_png) && file.exists(eq_png)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_path("fig_equivalence_forest.png"))
} else {
  cat("*Figure: fig_equivalence_forest.png not found. Run `Rscript 07_manuscript/chapter2/scripts/plot_equivalence_forest.R`.*")
}
```

## Subject-Level PF–Pupil Coupling {#sec-subject-coupling}

```{r subject-coupling-values}
#| include: false
get_coupling_n <- function(tsk) {
  if (is.null(pf_pupil_correlations)) return(NA_integer_)
  v <- pf_pupil_correlations$n[pf_pupil_correlations$task == tsk]
  if (length(v) == 0L) return(NA_integer_)
  suppressWarnings(max(v, na.rm = TRUE))
}
n_adt_coupling <- get_coupling_n("ADT")
n_vdt_coupling <- get_coupling_n("VDT")
```

Subject-level coupling asks whether participants with larger effort-evoked pupil changes also showed larger effort-evoked shifts in their psychometric functions (@sec-subject-coupling-methods). That double requirement is why the sample here (ADT *n* = `r n_adt_coupling`, VDT *n* = `r n_vdt_coupling`) is smaller than either analytic stream on its own. Hypothesis 4 predicted that participants with stronger effort-evoked arousal responses would show larger threshold increases and larger slope reductions.

Dashed line = no coupling (*r* = 0). The VDT Cognitive AUC × threshold point (open ring) is outlier-sensitive; the panel annotation reports *r* after excluding influential cases.", n_adt_coupling, n_vdt_coupling)
```{r subject-coupling-forest-fig}
#| fig-width: 9
```
