```{r subject-coupling-forest-fig}
}
```

@fig-subject-coupling-forest places all eight task by pupil-metric by PF-parameter tests on one unitless axis (Pearson *r* with 95% CI). Every interval crosses zero. The visual correlations fall slightly left of zero and the auditory ones land on it, but that asymmetry is well inside sampling noise, and the wide, near-identical intervals show the study cannot resolve coupling this small at these sample sizes. Modality-specific scatter axes would have made the visual trend look stronger than it is; the full correlation table (@tbl-pf-pupil-correlations) and z-scored scatter overlays are in @sec-appendix-d.

Two checks confirm the null does not hinge on a few influential participants. Influence diagnostics (Cook's distance > 4/*n*, hat value > 2 times the mean, |DFBETAS| > 2/√*n*) flagged a handful of cases whose Δ scores traced back to unstable per-condition fits, with differences as large as +19 Hz in threshold and −11 in slope. The one correlation large enough to invite a story, VDT Cognitive AUC by threshold (*r* = −0.169), fell to *r* = −0.028 once those cases were dropped, and Spearman ρ told the same story (@tbl-coupling-sensitivity, @sec-appendix-d). H4 therefore finds no reliable subject-level coupling in either modality.

The full pairwise correlation matrix across ΔCognitive AUC, ΔTotal AUC, ΔThreshold, and ΔSlope is shown in @sec-appendix-d, together with z-scored scatter overlays for raw Δ clouds on shared axes.

One exploratory pattern deserves note: a significant negative association emerged between effort-evoked changes in Cognitive AUC and Total AUC (r = −0.352, p < .01), so participants with larger total-arousal increases under High effort showed larger *reductions* in task-evoked cognitive pupil response. Because this pattern comes from the broader subject-level correlation matrix rather than a focal confirmatory hypothesis test, it should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive evidence for suppression or reallocation.

```{r h4-results-interpretation, results = "asis"}
h4 <- h4_coupling_summary
if (!is.null(h4) && !identical(h4$primary_statistic, "—")) {
  cat(
    "For H4, subject-level Δpupil–ΔPF correlations were uniformly small (",
    h4$primary_statistic,
    "; @fig-subject-coupling-forest). ",
    h4$support_status,
    "\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*H4 coupling statistics unavailable.*\n\n")
}
```

# Discussion

## Integration with Theoretical Frameworks

At the primary quality tier, the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction was not significant, and the equivalence test ruled out effects exceeding ±0.10 probit units (@sec-pupil-quality-tier). That combination supports a bounded null: the data do not show reliable coupling, and large effects are statistically incompatible with the primary-tier estimate. Whether small coupling exists remains unresolvable at the present sample size (see @sec-power-analysis). The sign of the interaction is not stable across sensitivity checks (@sec-pupil-quality-tier), so neither supra-optimal impairment nor moderate-arousal enhancement follows from these estimates. High effort shifted overall responding in @tbl-pupil-psychometric—a tendency change more than a clear sensitivity loss—and pupil trait was null (H3c). Because the coupling test used a phasic, stimulus-locked metric rather than tonic baseline diameter, the design cannot separate weak true coupling from a suboptimal index of LC-linked gain (@fig-mechanism).

Because trial-wise pupil state did not predict sensitivity beyond effort condition, the present data do not support trial-level arousal modulation of psychometric steepness in this sample. The effort main effect in @tbl-pupil-psychometric may reflect dual-task interference, group-level arousal, strategic responding, or some mix; resource-competition accounts are compatible but not uniquely supported.

```{r mechanism-fig}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Theoretical mechanisms of effort-induced pupil dissociation.
#|   **(A) Observed dissociation.** High-effort handgrip (red) elevates overall arousal (Total AUC) while simultaneously blunting the task-evoked pupil response (Cognitive AUC) in the stimulus-locked cognitive window (4.85--6.05 s), relative to low effort (blue).
#|   **(B) Phasic suppression.** Under this account, the neural resources sustained to maintain 40% MVC grip actively inhibit the gain of the LC--NE phasic response to task-relevant targets, producing the blunted cognitive-window response despite elevated baseline arousal.
#|   **(C) Baseline-correction asymmetry.** Cognitive AUC subtracts a pre-target baseline (B1) that itself rises under High effort, mechanically compressing the cognitive metric even when raw pupil diameter remains elevated; Total AUC instead references pre-squeeze B0, which did not shift with effort in this sample.
#|   **(D) Age-related shift to supra-optimal zone.** A stylised Yerkes--Dodson representation showing how an age-related leftward shift of the optimal arousal zone makes older adults more vulnerable to performance decrements in high-effort contexts, consistent with the non-significant coupling observed here.
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

mech_path <- file.path(chapter2_dir, "output", "figures", "mechanism.png")
if (file.exists(mech_path)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(mech_path)
} else {
  alt <- file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", "mechanism.png")
  if (file.exists(alt)) {
    knitr::include_graphics(alt)
  } else {
    cat("*Figure: mechanism.png not found. Expected at:* ", mech_path)
  }
}
```

## Implications for Aging and Arousal

The present data show weaker pupil–sensitivity coupling than predicted. The trial-level interaction was non-significant and, by the equivalence test, statistically negligible relative to the SESOI, and the subject-level correlations were uniformly small (@fig-subject-coupling-forest). The one correlation large enough to suggest a modality difference—VDT threshold—fell to near zero once a few influential participants were removed (@sec-subject-coupling). So the subject-level results carry little weight on their own; the strongest claim the data support is the bounded trial-level null. When Chapter 1 reports coupling in younger adults on the same continuous-intensity GLMM, that cross-chapter contrast will be a direct test of age-related attenuation of LC–NE gain modulation [@lee2018; @mather2016]. A second reading, not mutually exclusive, is that the effort-related response shift in @tbl-pupil-psychometric alongside the null interaction reflects older adults treating high-effort demand as contextual load rather than something that reshapes moment-to-moment arousal–sensitivity coupling.

The observed dissociation between elevated Total AUC and attenuated Cognitive AUC under high effort (@sec-manipulation-check) reflects both sustained effort-related dilation and metric-specific baseline choice (see @fig-mechanism). One possibility (@fig-mechanism, panel B) is phasic suppression: the neural resources required to maintain a 40% MVC grip actively compete with, or inhibit the gain of, the LC–NE phasic response to the target stimulus, producing a smaller incremental dilation above the pre-target level despite elevated overall arousal. A complementary account (@fig-mechanism, panel C) is baseline-correction asymmetry: B1 rises under High effort while B0 does not, so the B1-corrected Cognitive AUC can fall even when raw pupil diameter in the cognitive epoch remains elevated. Both mechanisms would produce lower Cognitive AUC under high effort, but only the first implies a genuine attenuation of task-evoked neuromodulatory response. Empirically distinguishing them would require reporting raw (uncorrected) pupil levels alongside corrected metrics, or fitting deconvolution-based tonic/phasic models.

Either reading fits the leftward shift on the Yerkes–Dodson curve in @fig-mechanism (panel D). If older adults' optimal zone sits at lower objective demand, a 40% MVC context may land them past the peak, degrading fine-grained trial-by-trial modulation even when group-level response tendency shifts under load (@tbl-pupil-psychometric).

At the same time, subject-level changes in Cognitive AUC and Total AUC were negatively correlated across participants (@sec-subject-coupling; r = −0.352, p < .01), indicating that larger effort-evoked total arousal co-occurred with larger *reductions* in task-evoked cognitive pupil response. This exploratory pattern parallels the @sec-manipulation-check dissociation and is consistent with a suppression or reallocation account, but it should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings. Pupil data quality varies across older adults due to factors such as eye-tracking challenges, increased blink rates, and age-related changes in pupil dynamics. The reported analyses therefore use tiered validity filters (primary, lenient, strict) and test whether conclusions are robust to stricter or more permissive inclusion criteria. Expanded gap-aware quality metrics were developed for this project and remain useful for future refinements, but they were not the operative gates for the saved model objects reported here. Even with quality filtering, some participants had limited usable pupil data, which reduced power for detecting state-level effects.

### Missingness and selection bias {#sec-missingness-limitation}

Missingness was non-random: High-effort trials had significantly higher odds of usable pupil data than Low-effort trials (OR = 1.203, *p* < .001), and VDT trials had nearly twice the odds of usable data compared to ADT trials (OR = 1.967, *p* < .001; @sec-missingness). This means the analysis samples are not identical across conditions, introducing potential selection bias. The effort-direction effect (more data retained under High effort, likely due to reduced blinking during demanding grip) does not obviously favour the null hypothesis, but the modality difference (far more ADT data missing) limits the symmetry of cross-task comparisons. Missingness was not predicted by stimulus intensity (*p* = .565) or response time (*p* = .982), suggesting that the psychometric intensity structure of retained trials is not systematically distorted. However, these diagnostics do not rule out missing-not-at-random mechanisms in which the physiological state being indexed by the pupil itself contributes to track loss or blink-related dropout. The robustness checks across quality tiers (@sec-appendix-b) further indicate that primary-tier findings are not uniquely driven by the specific inclusion threshold, though systematic missingness remains an inherent limitation of older-adult pupillometry in this paradigm.

The PF-based behavioral backbone also has important design limitations. Individual Weibull fits were estimated with free guess and lapse parameters from a small number of stimulus levels per condition, which can leave slope estimates weakly constrained at the participant level when the effective stimulus grid is coarse. Cross-checking against raw Psignifit `.mat` outputs can still be useful for boundary- or lapse-driven behavior in individual participants.

### Post-hoc power analysis {#sec-power-analysis}

```{r sample-size-power-limitation}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

# Design info and interaction SE from primary GLMM (Wald-based sensitivity analysis)
mod_primary_path <- file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_primary.rds")
se_int <- NA_real_
est_int <- NA_real_
n_trials <- NA_integer_
n_sub <- NA_integer_

if (!is.null(glmm_primary_sample)) {
  n_trials <- glmm_primary_sample$n_trials
  n_sub <- glmm_primary_sample$n_sub
}

if (file.exists(mod_primary_path)) {
  mod_primary <- readRDS(mod_primary_path)
  fe <- broom.mixed::tidy(mod_primary, effects = "fixed")
  ir <- fe %>% dplyr::filter(term == "stimulus_intensity_scaled:pupil_cognitive_state_scaled")
  if (nrow(ir) == 1L) {
    se_int <- ir$std.error[1]
    est_int <- ir$estimate[1]
  }
  fr_n <- nrow(stats::model.frame(mod_primary))
  if (!is.na(fr_n) && (is.na(n_trials) || n_trials != fr_n)) {
    warning("GLMM model.frame N (", fr_n, ") differs from glmm_primary_sample (", n_trials, ")")
  }
}
if (is.na(se_int) && !is.null(pupil_psychometric_effects)) {
  ir <- pupil_psychometric_effects %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "stimulus_intensity_scaled:pupil_cognitive_state_scaled")
  if (nrow(ir) == 1L) {
    se_int <- ir$std.error[1]
    est_int <- ir$estimate[1]
  }
}
if (is.na(n_trials) && !is.null(merged_data)) {
  gs <- summarize_glmm_primary_sample(merged_data)
  n_trials <- gs$n_trials
  n_sub <- gs$n_sub
}

mean_tr <- if (!is.null(glmm_primary_sample)) {
  round(glmm_primary_sample$mean_trials_per_sub, 1)
} else if (!is.na(n_trials) && !is.na(n_sub) && n_sub > 0L) {
  round(n_trials / n_sub, 1)
} else {
  NA_real_
}

z_a <- stats::qnorm(0.975)
z_b <- stats::qnorm(0.8)
beta_min <- (z_a + z_b) * se_int
lam <- est_int / se_int
post_pow_two <- stats::pnorm(lam - z_a) + stats::pnorm(-lam - z_a)
se_tgt <- abs(est_int) / (z_a + z_b)
n_mult <- if (!is.na(se_int) && se_tgt > 0) (se_int / se_tgt)^2 else NA_real_
n_participants_equiv <- if (!is.na(n_mult) && !is.na(n_sub)) round(n_sub * n_mult) else NA_integer_

n_quality_trials <- if (!is.null(quality_primary_trials)) {
  sum(quality_primary_trials$n_trials)
} else {
  NA_integer_
}

para <- paste0(
  "To put the non-significant primary interaction in context, we conducted a sensitivity power analysis ",
  "estimating the minimum detectable effect size (MDE) given the present design. ",
  "Using the observed design parameters---",
  if (is.na(n_sub)) "[N]" else format(n_sub, big.mark = ","), " participants ",
  "contributing a mean of ",
  if (is.na(mean_tr)) "[X]" else sprintf("%.1f", mean_tr),
  " complete-case primary-tier trials each (total ",
  if (is.na(n_trials)) "[N_trials]" else format(n_trials, big.mark = ","),
  " GLMM observations; ",
  if (is.na(n_quality_trials)) "[N_quality]" else format(n_quality_trials, big.mark = ","),
  " trials passed the quality gate before complete-case filtering)---",
  "with $\\alpha$ = .05 and 80% power, the MDE for the stimulus intensity × pupil state interaction ",
  "(standardized probit coefficient) was approximately $\\beta_{\\min}$ = ",
  if (is.na(beta_min)) "[X.XXX]" else sprintf("%.3f", beta_min), ". ",
  "The obtained coefficient (",
  if (is.na(est_int)) "$\\beta$ = +0.035" else paste0("$\\beta$ = ", sprintf("%+.3f", est_int)),
  ") falls well below this threshold. ",
  "The study therefore lacked the precision to distinguish a coupling of this magnitude from zero; ",
  "detecting an effect as small as the point estimate would require roughly ",
  if (is.na(n_mult)) "[X.X]" else sprintf("%.1f", n_mult),
  " times the current effective sample size (on the order of ",
  if (is.na(n_participants_equiv)) "XX" else format(n_participants_equiv, big.mark = ","),
  " participants). ",
  "The SESOI for the equivalence test was pre-specified at $\\pm$0.10 probit units, slightly above this MDE (@sec-sesoi-rationale). ",
  "Equivalence (@sec-pupil-quality-tier) and sensitivity power therefore address complementary parts of the same question: ",
  "effects larger than the SESOI are statistically incompatible with the primary-tier 90\\% CI, ",
  "whereas effects between the point estimate and the MDE remain unresolvable at the present sample size. ",
  "Together, the data are best described as a bounded null: large coupling is excluded, ",
  "but whether any small true effect exists cannot be determined without substantially larger samples ",
  "and improved pupil data retention."
)
cat(para)
```

### Equivalence bound rationale {#sec-sesoi-rationale}

```{r sesoi-anchors}
#| echo: false

sesoi_b1 <- if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_effects)) {
  b1 <- pupil_psychometric_effects %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "stimulus_intensity_scaled") %>%
    dplyr::pull(estimate)
  if (length(b1) == 1L) b1 else 1.31
} else {
  1.31
}
sesoi_pct_slope <- if (is.finite(sesoi_b1) && sesoi_b1 != 0) 100 * 0.10 / abs(sesoi_b1) else 7.6
sesoi_mde <- if (exists("beta_min") && !is.na(beta_min)) beta_min else 0.085
```

The pre-specified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) for the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction was set to $\pm 0.10$ probit units on the standardized latent scale used in the primary GLMM. Three considerations governed this choice.

The primary anchor is resource-based. Following @lakens2017, a SESOI can be grounded in what the achieved design can reliably resolve given $\alpha$, power, and sample size. At the primary quality tier, the minimum detectable effect for the interaction (@sec-power-analysis) was approximately $\beta_{\min}$ = `r sprintf("%.3f", sesoi_mde)`. The SESOI was set slightly above this MDE (0.10 > `r sprintf("%.3f", sesoi_mde)`), so equivalence claims are conservative relative to the study's resolving power: we require coupling to fall within a margin beyond what precision alone would permit, rather than declaring equivalence at the edge of detectability.

Two secondary anchors corroborate that magnitude. First, 0.10 corresponds to roughly `r sprintf("%.1f", sesoi_pct_slope)`% of the main intensity slope ($\beta_1 \approx$ `r sprintf("%.2f", sesoi_b1)`), a shift in psychometric steepness that would be noticeable if pupil state spanned the full standardized range. Second, because the model uses a probit link, fixed effects are on a standard-normal latent scale, so Cohen's conventional benchmarks for standardized mean differences apply directly [@cohen1988]; the SESOI of 0.10 is half of Cohen's "small" effect (0.20). We treat that convention as corroborating only—it is widely criticized as arbitrary and is not our sole justification.

No published trial-level GLMM has reported a pupil-state × intensity *sensitivity* interaction on a comparable probit scale, so an external empirical prior could not be imported directly. Prior pupil–behavior work more often links phasic arousal to decision *bias* or criterion (@deGee2020pupil; @colizoli2018belief) than to psychometric slope—a pattern consistent with the present dissociation between a reliable effort main effect on overall responding and a null slope interaction. Equivalence testing therefore asks whether the data are compatible with coupling effects smaller than the SESOI, not merely whether the frequentist null can be rejected.

The primary cognitive pupil metric uses a fixed 1.20-second stimulus-locked window (4.85–6.05 s) to reduce RT confounding and capture the TEPR peak. The grip is released during the post-probe blank (~4.45 s), so the window begins approximately 400 ms after release and does not overlap the effort manipulation itself. It does, however, overlap the response screen (4.70 s, appearing 150 ms before the window opens) and button presses at variable times (median `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_rt) else "—"` s after response-screen onset, or `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_press) else "—"` s after squeeze onset). These create potential confounds from attentional responses to the response screen and motor/blink artifacts from the button press.

Several mitigation strategies are implemented. Mean dilation (AUC/duration) is used rather than raw AUC to remove duration confounds; sensitivity analyses use slow-RT trials where motor cannot contaminate the primary window; and motor-buffered and pre-response window definitions are computed and available for future sensitivity analyses when full AUC computation is completed. However, complete elimination of temporal overlap confounds is impossible given the task design, and the primary window represents a trade-off between capturing relevant arousal dynamics and minimizing measurement artifacts. Response-locked metrics (available for future sensitivity analyses) can capture decision-related arousal more directly but are more susceptible to RT confounding. The choice of window definition represents a trade-off between physiological validity and measurement confounds.

The slow-RT sensitivity subset (trials with RT > 1.5 s, where button press falls outside the cognitive window) yielded an interaction estimate of opposite sign relative to the primary-tier result (@sec-pupil-quality-tier). Although neither estimate is statistically significant, the sign reversal indicates that motor or response-screen contamination of the cognitive window plausibly contributed to the positive direction of the primary-tier point estimate. This prevents a clean attribution of even the non-significant positive trend to genuine arousal–sensitivity coupling. Future analyses using motor-buffered or response-locked pupil windows (@sec-appendix-e) would provide a cleaner test.

## Integration with Chapter 1 and Chapter 3

```{r integration-ch1-ch2-coupling, results = "asis"}
h4_txt <- if (!is.null(h4_coupling_summary) &&
                !identical(h4_coupling_summary$primary_statistic, "—")) {
  h4_coupling_summary$primary_statistic
} else {
  "near zero"
}
cat(
  "Chapter 2 extends the dual-task paradigm from younger adults (Chapter 1) to older adults. ",
  "In Chapter 2, trial-level pupil × sensitivity coupling was not statistically reliable at the primary quality tier, ",
  "and subject-level Δpupil–ΔPF correlations were uniformly small (",
  h4_txt,
  "). ",
  "Chapter 1 will provide the younger-adult benchmark for direct comparison; the comparison matters because Chapter 1 used the same continuous-intensity GLMM framework and the same Total AUC / Cognitive AUC decomposition, so any difference in coupling magnitude between chapters can be attributed to age rather than to methodological divergence.\n\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

Several contrasts between the two chapters bear on the interpretation of the present null. In Chapter 1, Total AUC increased with effort across all three tasks (visual working memory, auditory discrimination, visual discrimination), confirming that 40% MVC grip reliably raises overall arousal in healthy younger adults. Cognitive AUC in that sample was treated as exploratory because the measurement window was short and only partially captured the TEPR peak; effects were smaller and less consistent. The present chapter improves on that design in two ways: the cognitive window is fixed at 4.85–6.05 s to align with the expected TEPR peak, and the analysis adds the continuous-intensity GLMM coupling test that Chapter 1 did not include.

Whether Chapter 1 shows trial-level pupil–sensitivity coupling in younger adults is an open question at this stage. If it does, the contrast with the bounded null here fits a straightforward story about aging: older adults' LC–NE system, already degraded structurally [@mather2016], may not generate the fine-grained phasic gain modulation that drives within-trial arousal–sensitivity coupling in younger adults. If coupling is absent in both chapters, the shared null points instead to limitations of the metric or task design. Either way, the side-by-side comparison is the strongest test of the age-related hypothesis, and the present chapter documents the older-adult side of it in full.

Chapter 3 will apply hierarchical drift diffusion modeling to decompose the behavioral patterns here into latent decision parameters—drift rate, boundary separation, starting point, and non-decision time. That decomposition will test whether the effort main effect on "different" responding (a response-tendency shift, not a sensitivity decrement by the present analysis) maps onto boundary adjustment, lower drift rate, or some combination. It will also clarify whether any arousal-linked effects, however small, trace back to evidence quality or to strategic control—a question the psychometric framework alone cannot fully resolve.

## Conclusions and Future Directions

Chapter 2 provides a systematic characterization of how pupil-indexed arousal covaries with psychophysical decision behavior in older adults, using continuous stimulus intensity modeling and within-subject centering to preserve individual arousal granularity. The findings contribute to understanding whether physical effort–induced arousal modulates perceptual sensitivity at the trial level, and whether this relationship is robust across data quality thresholds and model specifications.

Future work could test whether alternative pupil windows (motor-buffered, pre-response, or response-locked summaries) show clearer arousal–sensitivity coupling once full AUCs are computed; compare younger and older adults on the same coupling question; use the computational models in Chapter 3 to link behavior to latent decision parameters; and apply event-based GLM or deconvolution to separate target-, response-screen-, and motor-related pupil components.

The work presented here establishes the empirical and methodological foundation for Chapter 3, which will examine whether latent decision parameters provide a coherent mechanistic account of how physical effort and arousal reshape perceptual decisions in aging.

# Appendix

## Appendix A: Gap-Aware QC Metric Specifications {#sec-appendix-a}

In addition to percentage-validity thresholds, gap-aware quality control metrics identify trials with problematic missing-data patterns. Percentage-validity thresholds are necessary but not sufficient: a trial can have acceptable overall validity (e.g., 60%) but contain large contiguous gaps that distort AUC estimates. Following @kret2019preprocessing, each trial carried **`cog_auc_max_gap_ms`** (longest contiguous missing segment in the cognitive window in ms; gaps over 250 ms should not be interpolated and can distort AUC even when percent-valid looks acceptable), **`cog_window_duration`** (realized cognitive-window duration in seconds, which should stay near 1.20 s for the fixed window), **`cog_auc_n_valid`** (count of non-NA samples; ~300 at 250 Hz over 1.20 s), **`cog_auc_n_segments`** (number of contiguous valid segments, where fragmentation flags unreliable AUC), and **`cog_auc_prop_valid`** (valid samples divided by expected count at 250 Hz). Together these metrics help separate **genuine low dilation** (clean data, small gaps) from **artifactual lows** (gaps or fragmentation), so acceptable physiology is retained and problematic trials can be excluded.

## Appendix B: Robustness Checks — Model Comparison and Supplementary Tables {#sec-appendix-b}

Quality-tier interaction estimates and the interpretation that the effect is not robust at the primary tier are summarized in @sec-pupil-quality-tier. The appendix below provides AIC comparison, the slow-RT subset refit, and the model-predicted psychometric figure.

```{r appendix-b-table8}
#| label: tbl-appendix-aic-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Model Comparison: With vs. Without Interaction Term"

mod_w <- file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_primary.rds")
mod_wo <- file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_no_interaction.rds")
if (file.exists(mod_w) && file.exists(mod_wo)) {
  aw <- stats::AIC(readRDS(mod_w))
  ao <- stats::AIC(readRDS(mod_wo))
  daic <- aw - ao
  tibble::tibble(
    Model = c(
      "Without interaction",
      "With interaction",
      "Delta AIC (With minus Without)"
    ),
    Value = c(ao, aw, daic)
  ) %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Model / contrast", "AIC"),
      digits = 2
    )
} else {
  cat("*AIC comparison: model RDS files not found.*")
}
```

Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) comparison addresses whether the stimulus intensity $\times$ pupil-state interaction improves fit beyond the main-effects structure. A lower AIC for the model **without** the interaction indicates that the interaction does not improve fit enough to offset its complexity; in the present analysis, the no-interaction model fit marginally better ($\Delta$AIC = +0.66 for adding the interaction).

```{r tbl-tost-equivalence}
#| label: tbl-tost-equivalence

if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_tost) && nrow(pupil_psychometric_tost)) {
  pupil_psychometric_tost %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      Analysis = analysis_label,

    ) %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Analysis", "beta (probit)", "90% CI", "p (Wald)", "Inside +/-0.10?"),
      align = c("l", "r", "c", "r", "c")
    )
} else if (file.exists(file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_primary.rds"))) {
  build_interaction_tost_summary(models_dir) %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      Analysis = analysis_label,
      `beta (probit)` = sprintf("%+.3f", estimate),
      `90% CI` = sprintf("[%+.3f, %+.3f]", ci90_lower, ci90_upper),
      `p (Wald)` = vapply(p_wald, format_equiv_p, character(1L)),
      `Inside +/-0.10?` = vapply(inside_sesoi, format_inside_sesoi, character(1L))
    ) %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Analysis", "beta (probit)", "90% CI", "p (Wald)", "Inside +/-0.10?"),
      align = c("l", "r", "c", "r", "c")
    )
} else {
  cat("*TOST equivalence table not yet available.*")
}
```

**Exploratory tertile psychometric functions.** @fig-appendix-b2-tertiles shows binned proportion-"different" curves split by within-trial pupil tertile (Low / Medium / High cognitive pupil state). This figure is descriptive only: binning can suggest separation even when the primary GLMM interaction is small and non-significant, and it should not be used as confirmatory evidence for coupling.

Model-predicted psychometric functions at low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD) within-subject pupil cognitive state (@fig-appendix-b1-predicted) can appear visually separated even when the interaction coefficient is small and non-significant; such plots rely on extrapolation across the full scaled intensity range and should not be interpreted as evidence of a reliable effect without corroborating statistical evidence.

```{r appendix-b-fig-b1}
#| label: fig-appendix-b1-predicted
#| fig-cap: >

#|   response as a function of scaled stimulus intensity, for within-subject pupil cognitive state
#|   held at $-1$, $0$, and $+1$ SD (Low / Medium / High pupil; trait fixed at mean).
#|   Caution: Visual separation between curves reflects model extrapolation across the full intensity range.
#|   The underlying interaction coefficient was small and non-significant
#|   ($\beta = +0.035$, 95\% CI $[-0.024, +0.095]$, $p = .245$, $\Delta$AIC $= 0.66$);
#|   this figure should not be interpreted as evidence of a reliable effect.

# Primary pipeline saves this from `04_pupil_psychometric_coupling/06_pupil_psychometric_coupling.R`

)

}
```

**Pre-specified slow-RT sensitivity (motor overlap).** The primary cognitive window overlaps the response screen and typical button presses (@sec-response-timing). A pre-specified sensitivity analysis restricted the GLMM to trials where the button press fell entirely outside the cognitive window (RT > 1.5 s; motor-uncontaminated subset), so motor execution could not contaminate the pupil epoch. The stimulus intensity $\times$ pupil state interaction was non-significant and opposite in sign to the primary-tier estimate (@sec-pupil-quality-tier). The small positive interaction at the primary tier therefore cannot rule out motor overlap as a partial contributor; the slow-RT subset is consistent with unknown sign for any true effect.

```{r appendix-b-slow-rt-table}
#| label: tbl-appendix-slow-rt
#| tbl-cap: "Slow-RT Sensitivity Subset: Fixed Effects (Primary GLMM Structure)"

if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_slow_rt)) {
  slow_rt_labels <- c(
    "(Intercept)"                                              = "Intercept",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled"                                = "Stimulus Intensity",
    "pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil State (within-person)",
    "effort_factorHigh"                                        = "Effort: High vs. Low",
    "task_factorVDT"                                           = "Task: VDT vs. ADT",
    "pupil_cognitive_trait_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil Trait (between-person)",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled:pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"   = "Stimulus Intensity × Pupil State"
  )
  pupil_psychometric_slow_rt %>%
    dplyr::mutate(term = dplyr::recode(term, !!!slow_rt_labels)) %>%
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "SE", "z", "p"),
      digits = 4
    )
} else {
  cat("*Slow-RT model effects not available.*")
}
```

```{r subject-coupling-sensitivity}
      align = c("l", "l", "r", "c", "r", "r", "r", "c")
```

## Appendix E: Pre-Specified Future Sensitivity Windows {#sec-appendix-e}

For **motor-buffered** analyses, window definitions truncate the primary cognitive window 150 ms before the button press (endpoint stored as `cog_win_primary_end_motorbuffered`), reducing motor-, movement-, and blink-related contamination; full AUC extraction requires re-processing trial-level files with RT and is left for future work. A **pre-response** definition instead aligns a decision window to the last 500 ms before the response (excluding the final 150 ms), targeting decision-related arousal with minimal motor overlap; that pipeline likewise awaits full re-processing. These definitions are documented for reproducibility and were **not** analyzed in the present chapter.

## Appendix F: Behavioral Psychometric-Function Descriptives {#sec-appendix-f}

Descriptive threshold and slope estimates by task and effort condition (PF-valid sample; @sec-analytic-samples). The effort contrasts that test H1 appear in @tbl-pf-effort-test in the main text.

```{r pf-backbone}
#| label: tbl-pf-params
#| tbl-cap: "Psychometric Function Parameters by Task and Effort (descriptive means and SDs)"

if (!is.null(pf_params)) {
  pf_summary <- filter_pf_analysis(pf_params) %>%
    group_by(task, effort) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      threshold_mean = mean(threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
      threshold_sd = sd(threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
      slope_mean = mean(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      slope_sd = sd(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  pf_summary %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Task", "Effort", "N", "Threshold (M)", "Threshold (SD)", 
                   "Slope (M)", "Slope (SD)"),
      digits = 3
    )
} else {
  cat("*PF parameters not yet computed.*")
}
```
